s.dp: Communication › Swear, Put Under Oath, Vow
s.d: to demand that a person take an oath as to the truth of what is said or as to the certainty that one will carry out the request or command{N:001}
s.g: to put under oath; to insist that one take an oath; to require that one swear
s.c: It is extremely difficult to translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω in a literal manner, though in some contexts one can say ‘I put you under oath,’ but in a number of passages the person speaking is imploring and not necessarily in a position to command or insist. Therefore, in a passage such as ⟦Mark 5:7|Mark 5:7⟧, one may render the meaning idiomatically as ‘for God’s sake, I ask you, do not punish me.’ In ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:27|1 Thessalonians 5:27⟧ one may translate ‘in the name of the Lord, I ask you to read this letter to all the Christian brothers,’ and in ⟦Matthew 26:63|Matthew 26:63⟧ one may translate ‘in the name of the living God, I charge you, Tell us who you are.’|In most languages one may translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω by simply adding a causative component to terms meaning ‘to swear’ or ‘to take an oath.’ In other words, ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω may be rendered as ‘to cause a person to say under oath.’

s.dp: Communication › Swear, Put Under Oath, Vow
s.d: to demand that a person take an oath as to the truth of what is said or as to the certainty that one will carry out the request or command{N:001}
s.g: to put under oath; to insist that one take an oath; to require that one swear
s.c: It is extremely difficult to translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω in a literal manner, though in some contexts one can say ‘I put you under oath,’ but in a number of passages the person speaking is imploring and not necessarily in a position to command or insist. Therefore, in a passage such as ⟦Mark 5:7|Mark 5:7⟧, one may render the meaning idiomatically as ‘for God’s sake, I ask you, do not punish me.’ In ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:27|1 Thessalonians 5:27⟧ one may translate ‘in the name of the Lord, I ask you to read this letter to all the Christian brothers,’ and in ⟦Matthew 26:63|Matthew 26:63⟧ one may translate ‘in the name of the living God, I charge you, Tell us who you are.’|In most languages one may translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω by simply adding a causative component to terms meaning ‘to swear’ or ‘to take an oath.’ In other words, ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω may be rendered as ‘to cause a person to say under oath.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: to be seen by or to be visible to, in the sense of being within the range of sight
s.g: to be seen by; to be visible to

s.dp: Communication › Non-Verbal Communication
s.d: an event in which something appears vividly and credibly to the mind, although not actually present, but implying the influence of some divine or supernatural power or agency

s.dp: Household Activities
s.d: pertaining to being roasted, baked, or broiled
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to make a distinction as to whether something is cooked over an open fire or in an enclosed area such as an oven. Furthermore, cooking over an open fire frequently involves a distinction as to whether the cooking is by means of active flames or simply the result of hot coals.

s.dp: Plants › Fruit Parts of Plants
s.d: the mature fruit of plants (that is, fruit which is ready for use)
s.c: In this one occurrence of ὀπώρα in the NT, ‘ripe fruit’ is to be understood in a figurative sense of ‘good things.’

s.dp: Relations › Manner
s.d: a marker of an event indicating how something took place

s.dp: Relations › Purpose
s.d: a marker of purpose for events and states (sometimes occurring in highly elliptical contexts){N:002}
s.g: in order to; for the purpose of; so that

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Whom or What Spoken or Written About
s.d: a reference to an indefinite means

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὁράω<SDBG:ὁράω:000000>}[a] ‘to see,’ {D:24.1}) that which is seen{N:001}

s.dp: Communication › Non-Verbal Communication
s.d: an event in which something appears vividly and credibly to the mind, although not actually present, but implying the influence of some divine or supernatural power or agency

s.dp: Communication › Non-Verbal Communication
s.d: an event in which something appears vividly and credibly to the mind, although not actually present, but implying the influence of some divine or supernatural power or agency

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: that which appears or is seen
s.c: ὅρασις in ⟦Revelation 4:3|Revelation 4:3⟧ may be rendered in some languages as ‘as seen’ or ‘to the eyes’ or ‘to look at,’ for example, ‘and he who sat upon it was similar to a jasper stone to look at’ or ‘to look at the one who sat on it was like looking at a jasper stone.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: pertaining to that which can be seen
s.c: In a number of languages it may be wise to render ‘visible and invisible’ as an active expression with ‘people’ as the subject, for example, ‘all things were created by him … both those things which people can see and those things which people cannot see’ or ‘… what people can see and what they cannot see.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: to see{N:001}
s.c: As in a number of other contexts, ἀδελφοῖς in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:6|1 Corinthians 15:6⟧ may be rendered as ‘fellow believers’ or simply ‘believers.’

s.dp: Think › To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
s.d: to take special notice of something, with the implication of concerning oneself
s.g: to take notice of; to consider; to pay attention to; to concern oneself with
s.c: Though the terms ἐπιβλέπω, ἐπεῖδον (ἐφοράω), and ὁράω suggest as a result of their central meanings some measure of visual perception, what is involved in these specific contexts is much more than visual perception. The focus is actually upon intellectual activity and concern.

s.dp: Understand › Come To Understand
s.d: to come to understand as the result of perception
s.g: to understand; to perceive; to see; to recognize

s.dp: Association › Visit
s.d: to go to see a person on the basis of friendship and with helpful intent
s.g: to visit; to go to see

s.dp: Case › Experiencer
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὁράω<SDBG:ὁράω:000000>}[a] ‘to see,’ {D:24.1}) to experience an event or state, normally in negative expressions indicating what one will not experience

s.dp: Learn
s.d: to acquire information, with focus upon the event of perception
s.g: to learn about; to find out about

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Happen
s.d: to take responsibility for causing something to happen
s.g: to see to it that something happens; to arrange for something to happen

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Prompters of Attention
s.d: prompter of attention, which serves also to emphasize the following statement
s.g: look; listen; pay attention; come now; then

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Prompters of Attention
s.d: prompter of attention, which serves also to emphasize the following statement
s.g: look; listen; pay attention; come now; then

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Markers of Emphasis
s.d: a marker of strong emphasis, indicating complete validation of what is said
s.g: indeed; certainly; at all; at least; in any event

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: a relative state of anger
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘anger’ without indicating against whom the anger exists. For example, in ⟦1 Timothy 2:8|1 Timothy 2:8⟧ it might be possible to say ‘to pray without anger against anyone’ or ‘to pray without being angry at anyone.’

s.dp: Punish, Reward › Punish
s.d: divine punishment based on God’s angry judgment against someone
s.c: Though the focal semantic element in ὀργή is punishment, at the same time there is an implication of God’s anger because of evil. Therefore, it is possible in some languages to translate this expression in ⟦Romans 3:5|Romans 3:5⟧ as ‘God does not do wrong when he is angry and punishes us, does he?’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: to be relatively angry
s.g: to be full of anger; to be furious; to be angry

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: pertaining to a tendency to become angry

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › Specific Measures of Length
s.d: traditionally the measurement of a man’s arms stretched out horizontally, reckoned at approximately six feet or almost two meters and used as a technical, nautical term to measure the depth of water
s.c: If one adopts a metric system, the later expression in ⟦Acts 27:28|Acts 27:28⟧, namely, ὀργυιὰς δεκαπέντε ‘fifteen fathoms,’ may be rendered as ‘about thirty meters.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire Strongly
s.d: to eagerly desire to accomplish some goal or purpose{N:001}
s.g: to strive to attain; to aspire to; to eagerly long for

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Elevated Land Formations
s.d: pertaining to an area characterized by mountains or hills

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire Strongly
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to burn with intense desire) to have a strong, intense desire for something
s.g: to be inflamed with passion; to have a strong lust for; to be inflamed with lust
s.c: In some languages the equivalent idiom is ‘to boil with desire,’ ‘to feel hot in the genitals,’ or ‘to prefer to die rather than to do.’

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: to live a life of moral correctness
s.g: to live right; to live as one ought to
s.c: ὀρθοποδέω may be translated in a number of languages as ‘to live as one should.’

s.dp: Features of Objects › Straight, Crooked
s.d: pertaining to being straight in contrast to what is crooked{N:001}
s.c: The context of ⟦Hebrews 12:13|Hebrews 12:13⟧ is, of course, figurative.

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to make straight wheel tracks for the feet) to live or behave in strict conformance to a predetermined model for behavior
s.g: to live; to behave; to conduct oneself correctly

s.dp: Communication › Teach
s.d: to give accurate instruction
s.g: to teach correctly; to expound rightly

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: (derivative of ὄρθρος[a] ‘early morning,’ {D:67.187}) to get up early in the morning and go about one’s affairs
s.g: to get up early; to get up early and go

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: pertaining to being early in the morning
the early part of the daylight period

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Units of Time: Daybreak, Midday, Midnight, Late
s.d: the point of time when the day begins{N:001}

s.dp: True, False › Accurate, Inaccurate
s.d: pertaining to conforming closely to an accepted norm or standard

s.dp: Think › To Decide, To Conclude
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὁρίζω ‘to set limits on,’ not occurring in the NT) to come to a definite decision or firm resolve
s.g: to decide; to determine; to resolve

s.dp: Control, Rule › Assign to a Role or Function
s.d: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
s.g: to appoint; to designate; to assign; to give a task to

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Sociopolitical Areas
s.d: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration{N:001}
s.g: region; territory; land; district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
s.c: The meanings of γῆ, χώρα, κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

s.dp: Communication › Swear, Put Under Oath, Vow
s.d: to affirm the truth of a statement by calling on a divine being to execute sanctions against a person if the statement in question is not true (in the case of a deity taking an oath, his divine being is regarded as validating the statement)
s.g: to swear; to make an oath; oath
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific in referring to the swearing of an oath, for example, ‘to say something by calling upon God to listen’ or ‘to state that something is true and asking God to punish if it is not true’ or ‘to make God responsible for what one has said.’

s.dp: Communication › Swear, Put Under Oath, Vow
s.d: to affirm the truth of a statement by calling on a divine being to execute sanctions against a person if the statement in question is not true (in the case of a deity taking an oath, his divine being is regarded as validating the statement)
s.g: to swear; to make an oath; oath
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific in referring to the swearing of an oath, for example, ‘to say something by calling upon God to listen’ or ‘to state that something is true and asking God to punish if it is not true’ or ‘to make God responsible for what one has said.’

s.dp: Linear Movement › Movement with Speed
s.d: a fast movement from one place to another

s.dp: Psychological Faculties
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὁρμή ‘rushing motion,’ not occurring in the NT) the psychological faculty of will and impulse
s.c: This clause in ⟦James 3:4|James 3:4⟧ may also be rendered simply as ‘wherever the pilot wants it to go.’

s.dp: Think › To Decide, To Conclude
s.d: (an idiom, literally: an impulse happens) to make a decision to carry out some action, but with emphasis upon the impulse involved
s.g: to make up one’s mind; to decide; to determine

s.dp: Aspect › Rapidity, Suddenness
s.d: an event involving sudden force and possible violence

s.dp: Animals › Birds
s.d: any kind of bird, wild or domestic
s.c: All languages have at least some terms for birds, but there may be no generic term which identifies birds while excluding all other creatures which fly. For example, in some languages a term which includes all kinds of birds also includes flying insects and bats. However, since in most instances such a term has birds as its primary reference, it can usually be employed in contexts in which birds are more or less readily identified by other expressions in the passage. In other languages generic terms for birds may identify only certain classes of birds, for example, birds of prey, water birds, and birds of the forest.|In the NT occurrences of ὄρνεον, the reference is to unclean birds, either birds of prey or scavengers.

s.dp: Animals › Birds
s.d: any kind of bird, wild or domestic
s.c: All languages have at least some terms for birds, but there may be no generic term which identifies birds while excluding all other creatures which fly. For example, in some languages a term which includes all kinds of birds also includes flying insects and bats. However, since in most instances such a term has birds as its primary reference, it can usually be employed in contexts in which birds are more or less readily identified by other expressions in the passage. In other languages generic terms for birds may identify only certain classes of birds, for example, birds of prey, water birds, and birds of the forest.|In this only NT occurrence (with parallel), ὄρνις probably designates a hen.

s.dp: Space › Limits, Boundaries of Space
s.d: established or fixed boundaries

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Elevated Land Formations
s.d: a relatively high elevation of land, in contrast with {L:βουνός<SDBG:βουνός:000000>} hill ({D:1.48}), which is by comparison somewhat lower
s.c: Terms referring to mountains, hills, or mounds inevitably reflect the nature of the surrounding landscape. For example, in the flat marshlands of the Central Sudan, an elevation called Doleib Hill is only some three or four feet above the surrounding area, but in the Himalayas elevations of land some ten or twelve thousand feet are still regarded as hills in contrast with the mountains. In the choice of receptor language terms for ὄρος and βουνός (LN 1.48), one must seek expressions which suggest corresponding differences. What is important is relative size, not an exact correspondence to biblical geography. It may, however, be necessary in some instances to introduce a footnote to describe the approximate height of certain biblical mountains or hills.

s.dp: Physical Impact › Dig
s.d: to make a hole in the ground and to remove earth with some sharp-edged intrument (for example, a pick or spade)

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: an offspring whose parents either are no longer alive or no longer function as parents (as the result of having abandoned their offspring)
s.c: Some languages make a distinction in terms for ‘orphan’ by indicating whether the child has been abandoned or whether one or both of the parents are dead. In languages where some indication of relative age must be introduced in speaking of ‘orphans,’ it is preferable in ⟦James 1:27|James 1:27⟧ to use a term which pertains to young children.

s.dp: Association › Associate
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὀρφανός<SDBG:ὀρφανός:000000>}[a] ‘orphan,’ {D:10.40}) one who is without associates who may be of sustaining help

s.dp: Linear Movement › Dance
s.d: patterned rhythmic movements of the whole and/or parts of the body, normally to the accompaniment of music
s.c: In a number of languages there are highly specific terms for various types of dancing, and one must make certain that the appropriate expression is used. Some terms for dancing may refer only to erotic dances; others, to highly ritualized performances in drama or religious practice; and still others may refer to personal expressions of happiness, joy, or grief. Special care must be exercised in selecting a term which will fit the context.

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Relative Reference
s.d: a relative reference to any entity, event, or state, either occurring overtly in the immediate context or clearly implied in the discourse or setting
s.g: who; which; what; the one who; that which

s.dp: Relations › Equivalence
s.d: a marker of an explanation or a clarification in the same or a different language
s.c: In some languages one must make more specific the interpretation of a term in another language. For example, in ⟦Mark 3:17|Mark 3:17⟧ it may be necessary to translate ‘Boanerges, which in another language means Men of Thunder’ or ‘Boanerges, for which we would say, Men of Thunder.’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: indefinite and multiple points of time, simultaneous with other corresponding points of time

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Holy, Pure
s.d: pertaining to being holy in the sense of superior moral qualities and possessing certain essentially divine qualities in contrast with what is human{N:001}

s.dp: Religious Activities › Dedicate, Consecrate
s.d: pertaining to being dedicated or consecrated to the service of God
s.c: In some languages it is essential to distinguish between ἅγιος and ὅσιος when these refer to God (see LN 88.24) and when they refer to persons or objects which have been consecrated to the service of God. It is both theoretically and practically advantageous to make a significant distinction in meaning on the basis of these contextual differences which occur in the Greek NT. It is not difficult to translate ἅγιος and ὅσιος by expressions meaning ‘dedicated to God,’ ‘devout,’ ‘pious,’ etc., but it may be extremely difficult to translate ἅγιος and ὅσιος when applied to God. In some languages one can only use an expression such as ‘he who is truly God’ or ‘he who is in every respect God.’

s.dp: Communication › Promise
s.d: the divine matters which have been promised
s.c: It is also possible to understand τὰ ὅσια in ⟦Acts 13:34|Acts 13:34⟧ as meaning ‘divine decrees’ or ‘decrees made by God.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Holy, Pure
s.d: the quality of holiness as an expression of the divine in contrast with the human
s.c: For another interpretation of ὁσιότης in ⟦Luke 1:75|Luke 1:75⟧, see LN 53.45.

s.dp: Religious Activities › Dedicate, Consecrate
s.d: the state resulting from being dedicated to the service of God
s.c: For another interpretation of ὁσιότης in ⟦Luke 1:75|Luke 1:75⟧, see LN 88.25.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Holy, Pure
s.d: pertaining to being holy in the sense of superior moral qualities and possessing certain essentially divine qualities in contrast with what is human{N:001}

s.dp: Features of Objects › Fragrance, Odor
s.d: the scent or odor of a substance, whether agreeable or disagreeable

s.dp: Quantity › Many, Few [Countables]
s.d: pertaining to a comparative quantity of objects or events
s.g: as many as; as much as

s.dp: Quantity › Much, Little [Masses, Collectives, Extensions]
s.d: pertaining to a comparison of a quantity
s.g: as much as; as long as

s.dp: Degree › Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
s.d: a degree of correlative extent
s.g: to the degree that; to the same degree; as much as
s.c: Expressions involving correspondence of degrees must often be rather considerably restructured. For example, in the first part of ⟦Revelation 18:7|Revelation 18:7⟧ one may translate in some languages ‘she honored herself very much and lived in great luxury, and so give her very much suffering and grief.’ In the case of ⟦Hebrews 1:4|Hebrews 1:4⟧, one may translate ‘God gave his Son a name that was more important than the name of the angels; therefore, God’s Son is greater than the angels.’|One may also render this expression in ⟦Hebrews 8:6|Hebrews 8:6⟧ as ‘Christ’s ministry is better than the old to the same degree that the covenant he mediates is better.’|In ⟦Romans 11:13|Romans 11:13⟧ ὅσον is strengthened by ἐπί (see LN 78.51).

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
s.d: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time
s.c: The additon of ἐπί (degree, LN 78.51) and/or χρόνος (time, LN 67.78) reinforces this meaning of ὅσος.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.c: In some languages a distinction is made between bones as a part of a living body and bones from which the meat has been removed, for example, the bones of a skeleton. Note, for example, the reference to τὰ ὀστέα as the bones of Joseph in ⟦Hebrews 11:22|Hebrews 11:22⟧.

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Whom or What Spoken or Written About
s.d: a reference to an indefinite entity, event, or state
s.c: Often translated as ‘who’, which, or what, since these pronouns in English are often indefinite in meaning.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: pertaining to being made of baked clay

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Smell
s.d: the capacity or ability to smell

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the part of the human body above the hips and below the ribs, the customary place for tying a belt
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘waist’ is a term meaning literally ‘the middle.’

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the male genital organs (‘loins’ in traditional English translations)
s.c: A literal rendering of ‘he was still in the genitals of his father’ (⟦Hebrews 7:10|Hebrews 7:10⟧) might be regarded in a number of languages as being excessively specific and even vulgar. It is possible to render this passage as simply ‘he was not as yet born’ or ‘his father had not yet caused him to be conceived.’ In ⟦Acts 2:30|Acts 2:30⟧ (καρποῦ τῆς ὀσφύος αὐτοῦ ‘the fruit of his loins’) it may be best to translate ‘one of his descendants’ (see LN 10.34).

s.dp: Ready, Prepared
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to gird up the loins) to cause oneself to be in a state of readiness
s.g: to get ready; to prepare oneself
s.c: In the context of ⟦Ephesians 6:14|Ephesians 6:14⟧, however, it may be useful to preserve the extended figure of readiness for warfare beginning with ⟦Ephesians 6:13|Ephesians 6:13⟧ and extending through verse 17.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: an indefinite point or points of time, which may be roughly simultaneous to or overlap with another point of time (ὅταν[a] and ἐπάν may also imply some degree of uncertainty)

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time which is roughly simultaneous to or overlaps with another point of time

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: indefinite and multiple points of time, simultaneous with other corresponding points of time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
s.d: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time which is roughly simultaneous to or overlaps with another point of time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
s.d: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time

s.dp: Case › Content
s.d: a marker of discourse content, whether direct or indirect
s.c: The marking of direct and indirect discourse varies greatly from language to language. In some instances there is no marker at all; in other cases one marker precedes and another follows. In still other instances a repetition of an expression of speaking occurs at the end of a quotation, whether direct or indirect. In a number of languages written usage differs appreciably from spoken usage, because intonation so often marks introduced discourse in the spoken form of a language.

s.dp: Relations › Cause and/or Reason
s.d: a marker of cause or reason, based on an evident fact
s.g: because; since; for; in view of the fact that

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Markers of Identificational and Explanatory Clauses [Epexegetical]
s.d: a marker of identificational and explanatory clauses
s.g: that; namely; that is; namely that

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation
s.d: marker of negative propositions{N:001}

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Markers for an Affirmative Response to Questions
s.d: marker of an affirmative response to a question{N:002}

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation
s.d: a negative response to questions or statements or an emphatic negation of a statement

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation
s.d: a marker of emphatic negation{N:003}

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Markers for an Affirmative Response to Questions
s.d: a marker of a strongly emphatic affirmative response to a question

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Where, Somewhere, Everywhere
s.d: a reference to a position in space (often used with ἐάν or ἄν ‘ever,’ {D:71.8}, to mark an indefinite and unrestricted position in space)

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Relative Reference
s.d: a relative reference to a set of circumstances

s.dp: Communication › Mock, Ridicule
s.d: an exclamation of mocking and ridicule
s.c: Almost all languages have interjections or exclamatory expressions indicating ridicule. If such does not exist in a language, one can always translate this expression in ⟦Mark 15:29|Mark 15:29⟧ as ‘now what about you, you who are going to destroy the sanctuary and in three days build it up again!’

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: a state of intense hardship or distress
s.c: In some languages there may not be a noun for ‘disaster,’ but one can express the meaning of the Greek term οὐαί as ‘how greatly one will suffer’ or ‘what terrible pain will come to one.’

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation
s.d: a marker of strongly emphatic negation
s.g: no indeed; by no means; most certainly not

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation Combined with Clitics
s.d: combination of the negative particle {L:οὐ<SDBG:οὐ:000000>}[a] ‘not,’ {D:69.3}, and the postpositive conjunction {L:δέ<SDBG:δέ:000000>}[a] ‘and,’ {D:89.94}

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation Combined with Clitics
s.d: combination of the negative particle {L:οὐ<SDBG:οὐ:000000>}[a] {D:69.3}, and the postpositional particle {L:δέ<SDBG:δέ:000000>} ‘even,’ which does not occur with this sense as an independent graphic unit in the NT

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Whom or What Spoken or Written About
s.d: a negative reference to an entity, event, or state

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
s.d: an indefinite negated point of time
s.g: never; not ever; at no time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: the negation of extending time up to and beyond an expected point

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: the extension of time up to a point but not beyond

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Markers for an Affirmative Response to Questions
s.d: a marker of a somewhat more emphatic affirmative response

s.dp: Relations › Result
s.d: a marker of result, often implying the conclusion of a process of reasoning
s.g: so; therefore; consequently; accordingly; then; so then

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Markers of Emphasis
s.d: a marker of somewhat greater emphasis (in comparison with {L:μέν<SDBG:μέν:000001>}[b], {L:γέ<SDBG:γέ:000000>}, and {L:δή<SDBG:δή:000000>}, {D:91.6})

s.dp: Relations › Contrast
s.d: a marker of relatively weak contrast
s.c: In a context such as ⟦John 9:18|John 9:18⟧, ὅτι may also serve as a type of transition.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: the negation of extending time up to and beyond an expected point

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: tail of an animal or insect
s.c: In some languages it may be important to distinguish clearly between the tail of a mammal, a fish, and a creature such as the scorpion.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Above the Earth
s.d: (derivative of {L:οὐρανός<SDBG:οὐρανός:000001>}[b] heaven, {D:1.11}) related to or located in heaven
s.g: heavenly; in heaven; pertaining to heaven
s.c: The derivatives οὐράνιος and ἐπουράνιος are essentially equivalent to semantic compounds in that they combine a semantic element of heaven as a celestial abode with another semantic element specifying location or relationship. Frequently such terms are translated as ‘in heaven’ or ‘from heaven’ or ‘belonging to heaven.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (an idiom, literally: heavenly army) a large group or throng of angels
s.g: throng of angels; ranks of angels
s.c: There may be distinct objections to speaking of στρατιὰ οὐράνιος as being a ‘heavenly army,’ though undoubtedly in earlier times the thought of angels being God’s military force would have been quite appropriate. Therefore, in place of some expression which may refer to an army or military unit, it may be possible to translate στρατιὰ οὐράνιος as simply ‘many, many angels’ or ‘row after row of angels.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Above the Earth
s.d: the sky as a source or as a location from which implied movement takes place
s.c: οὐρανόθεν in ⟦Acts 14:17|Acts 14:17⟧ and ⟦Acts 26:13|Acts 26:13⟧ is somewhat ambiguous, for both events may be regarded as involving a semantic derivative of οὐρανός heaven (LN 1.11) rather than οὐρανός sky (LN 1.5). In ⟦Acts 14:17|Acts 14:17⟧ one might very well translate ‘he gives rain from heaven,’ since obviously the agent is God. Similarly, in ⟦Acts 26:13|Acts 26:13⟧ the light might come from heaven, since the light is presumably regarded as a supernatural phenomenon.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Above the Earth
s.d: space above the earth, including the vault arching high over the earth from one horizon to another, as well as the sun, moon, and stars
s.c: In ⟦Acts 2:5|Acts 2:5⟧ the expression ‘under the sky’ is better translated in a number of languages as ‘on earth,’ and in ⟦Hebrews 11:12|Hebrews 11:12⟧ ‘the stars of the sky’ is effectively rendered in many instances as ‘the stars up above,’ though in many languages ‘up above’ is not only redundant, but misleading, since it might suggest stars that would not be ‘up above.’ The area described by the phrase ἀπ’ ἄκρων οὐρανῶν ἕως τῶν ἄκρων αὐτῶν in ⟦Matthew 24:31|Matthew 24:31⟧ refers to the limits of the horizon regarded as the limits of the sky, but in many languages the equivalent is an expression dealing with the limits of the earth.|In some contexts οὐρανός ‘sky’ designates areas which in other languages are referred to by terms specifying only a part of the area above the earth. For example, a literal translation of ἐμβλέψατε εἰς τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ‘look at the birds of the sky’ (⟦Matthew 6:26|Matthew 6:26⟧) would in some languages refer only to those birds which fly particularly high in the sky, for example, eagles, vultures, and falcons. The Greek expression τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ simply designates wild birds in contrast with domestic fowl, such as chickens. Therefore, in translating ‘the birds of the sky,’ one may wish to use a general designation for all wild birds. See also LN 4.41.|The sky (οὐρανός) is also represented in the Scriptures as a dwelling place of certain supernatural beings, for the various stars and constellations were associated with supernatural forces (see στρατιὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, literally ‘the army of heaven,’ in ⟦Acts 7:42|Acts 7:42⟧: ὁ θεὸς … παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς λατρεύειν τῇ στρατιᾷ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ‘God … gave them over to worship the stars of the heaven’). In some languages, however, there is a problem with the rendering ‘stars of heaven,’ since such an expression might imply that there are types of stars which do not exist in the sky. Therefore, it is often more appropriate to translate στρατιὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ as simply ‘the stars.’ At the same time it is often advisable to introduce a marginal note to indicate that the stars were regarded as symbols of supernatural beings. One may also translate στρατιὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ as ‘supernatural beings in the sky’ or ‘powers that dwell in the sky’ (see LN 12.45).|The semantic equivalent of οὐρανός is in some instances merely an adverb meaning ‘up’ or ‘above.’ In other languages the various areas referred to by ούρανός must be designated by more specific terms or phrases, for example, ‘the region of the stars,’ ‘the place of the clouds,’ or ‘where the wind blows,’ as a way of designating at least three different areas which may be significant in certain types of contexts.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Above the Earth
s.d: the supernatural dwelling place of God and other heavenly beings (οὐρανός[b] also contains a component denoting that which is above or in the sky, but the element of abode is evidently more significant than location above the earth)
s.c: In a number of languages precisely the same term is used to designate both ‘sky’ and ‘heaven’ (as the abode of God). But in many instances a completely separate term must be employed in speaking of the dwelling place of God, for example, ‘where God lives’ or ‘where God is’ or ‘from where God governs.’ In some languages the term referring to ‘heaven’ is simply ‘the home above,’ and in one instance a designation of heaven refers primarily to a state, for example, ‘the life above.’|The phrase τρίτος οὐρανός ‘the third heaven’ is a fixed phrase referring to the abode of God (ἁρπαγέντα τὸν τοιοῦτον ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ ‘(a man) who was caught up as far as the third heaven’ ⟦2 Corinthians 12:2|2 Corinthians 12:2⟧), but in a number of languages it is extremely difficult to speak of ‘the third heaven,’ especially if one uses a term for ‘heaven’ which is ‘the abode of God.’ Therefore, in many instances τρίτος οὐρανός is translated as ‘heaven’ or ‘the abode of God,’ and if necessary, a footnote may be added in order to indicate the literal meaning of the Greek expression. If a literal rendering is employed, it is usually equivalent to ‘the third sky’ or ‘above two degrees of sky.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:οὐρανός<SDBG:οὐρανός:000001>}[b] ‘heaven,’ {D:1.11}) a reference to God based on the Jewish tendency to avoid using a name or direct term for God
s.c: A translation such as ‘I have sinned against God’ would seem to be so much simpler than ‘I have sinned against heaven,’ but in reality it is not easy to find a satisfactory expression for ‘sinning against God.’ It is, of course, possible to speak of ‘fighting against a person,’ but ‘to sin against a person’ involves a very complex relationship which often needs to be more clearly explained, for example, ‘I have sinned against what God has said’ or ‘I have sinned by doing what displeases God.’ In some languages a strictly literal rendering of ‘I have sinned against God’ might be understood in the sense of committing some kind of sin with God.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Universe, Creation
s.d: a more or less fixed phrase: the heavens and the earth, equivalent to a single lexical item: the totality of God’s creation
s.c: There may be certain complications involved in rendering ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ as ‘heaven and earth,’ since ‘heaven’ might be interpreted in some languages as referring only to the dwelling place of God himself. The referents in this passage are ‘the sky and the earth,’ in other words, all of physical existence, but not the dwelling place of God, for the latter would not be included in what is destined to pass away.

s.dp: Animals › Birds
s.d: (an idiom, literally: birds of the sky) wild birds in contrast with domesticated birds such as chickens
s.c: A literal rendering of πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, either as ‘birds of the air’ or ‘birds of the sky,’ may be misleading, since ‘birds of the air’ might imply that these are birds made out of air, and ‘birds of the sky’ might suggest they are birds which remain always in the sky. In some languages the equivalent expression is ‘birds of the trees’ or ‘birds of the winds.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: (an idiom, literally: army of heaven) the stars of heaven as symbols of various supernatural powers
s.c: Since ‘the stars of heaven’ serve primarily as symbols of certain heavenly supernatural powers, it may be appropriate in some languages to speak of ‘the spirits of the stars in the sky.’ See also LN 1.5.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: (an idiom, literally: under the sky) pertaining to being on the earth
s.c: ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν is essentially equivalent in reference to ἐπίγειος ‘on the earth’ (LN 1.41).

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person greeted in {S:04501600900004}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a man whose wife is referred to in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
Sensory Events and States › Hear
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:οὖς<SDBG:οὖς:000000>}[a] ‘ear,’ {D:8.24}) the activity of hearing

s.dp: Know › Not Able To Be Known, Secret
s.d: (idioms, literally: into the ear, and: to the ear) pertaining to what is known only by those who hear a particular message in private
s.c: A phrase such as ‘whatever you hear in secret’ may be rendered as ‘whatever you hear when no one else is listening.’|For another treatment of the phrase πρὸς τὸ οὖς λαλέω, see LN 33.91.

s.dp: Communication › Speak, Talk
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to speak to the ear) to speak quietly and presumably to a restricted audience
s.c: For another treatment of the phrase πρὸς τὸ οὖς, see LN 28.73.

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Hear
s.d: (an idiom, literally: hold the ears closed) to refuse to listen to what is being said
s.g: to refuse to listen; to refuse to pay attention
s.c: In some languages the refusal to hear may be expressed idiomatically as ‘they put their hands over their ears’ or ‘they closed their ears’ or ‘the words never entered their heads.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Hear
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to put into the ears) to listen carefully to, with the implication of not forgetting
s.c: For another interpretation of this idiom in ⟦Luke 9:44|Luke 9:44⟧, see LN 29.5.

s.dp: Memory and Recall › Storing of Information
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to place in the ears) to continue to bear something in mind
s.g: to bear in mind; to remember well; to not forget
s.c: For another interpretation of the idiom τίθεμαι εἰς τὰ ὦτα in ⟦Luke 9:44|Luke 9:44⟧, see LN 24.64.

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to hear heavily with the ears) to be mentally slow or dull in comprehending
s.g: to be slow to understand; to be mentally dull

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: (derivative of {L:εἰμί<SDBG:εἰμί:000002>}[c] ‘to exist,’ {D:13.69}) that which exists as property and wealth
s.c: In most contexts in which οὐσία occurs in non-biblical Greek, the reference is to considerable possessions or wealth, and accordingly it would be appropriate in ⟦Luke 15:12|Luke 15:12⟧ to speak of ‘estate.’

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation Combined with Clitics
s.d: a marker of coordinate negativized expressions (combination of the negative particle {L:οὐ<SDBG:οὐ:000000>}[a] {D:69.3}, and the postpositive conjunction {L:τέ<SDBG:τέ:000000>}[a] ‘and,’ {D:89.95}){N:001}

s.dp: Sequence
s.d: with reference to that which precedes

s.dp: Sequence
s.d: referring to that which follows (compare {D:61.9})

s.dp: Degree › Much, Little [Positive-Negative Degree]
s.d: a relatively high degree, presumably in keeping with the context

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Negation
s.d: a marker of a somewhat more emphatically negativized proposition

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Markers for an Affirmative Response to Questions
s.d: a marker of a somewhat more emphatic affirmative response

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Owe, Debt, Cancel
s.d: a person who is in debt

s.dp: Mode › Should, Ought
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὀφείλω<SDBG:ὀφείλω:000002>}[c] ‘to be under obligation,’ {D:71.25}) one who is obligated to do something
s.g: one who is obliged to; one who is obligated to; one who must

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὀφείλω<SDBG:ὀφείλω:000003>}[d] ‘to sin against,’ {D:88.298}) one who commits sin and thus incurs a moral debt

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Owe, Debt, Cancel
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὀφείλω<SDBG:ὀφείλω:000000>}[a] ‘to owe,’ {D:57.219}) that which is owed

s.dp: Mode › Should, Ought
s.d: that which ought to be done as a matter of duty or social obligation

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Owe, Debt, Cancel
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὀφείλω<SDBG:ὀφείλω:000000>}[a] ‘to owe,’ {D:57.219}) that which is owed
s.c: It is also possible to understand ὀφείλημα in ⟦Romans 4:4|Romans 4:4⟧ as meaning ‘obligation’ (see LN 71.26).

s.dp: Mode › Should, Ought
s.d: that which one must do out of a sense of duty or as the result of commitment
s.c: For another interpretation of ὀφείλημα in ⟦Romans 4:4|Romans 4:4⟧, see LN 57.221.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὀφείλω<SDBG:ὀφείλω:000003>}[d] ‘to sin against,’ {D:88.298}) the moral debt incurred as the result of sin

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Owe, Debt, Cancel
s.d: to be under obligation to make a payment as the result of having previously received something of value
s.g: to owe; to be in debt

s.dp: Mode › Necessary, Unnecessary
s.d: to be necessary or indispensable, with the implication of a contingency
s.g: must; have to; it is necessary

s.dp: Mode › Should, Ought
s.d: to be obligatory in view of some moral or legal requirement

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: to commit a sin against someone and thus to incur moral debt

s.dp: Mode › Should, Ought
s.d: that which ought to be if one only had one’s wish
s.c: In a number of languages it may be preferable to translate ὄφελον as simply an expression of wishing. Therefore, ⟦2 Corinthians 11:1|2 Corinthians 11:1⟧ might be rendered as ‘I wish you would grant me a bit of foolishness’ or ‘I wish you would tolerate a bit of foolishness on my part.’

s.dp: Value › Advantageous, Not Advantageous
s.d: pertaining to a benefit to be derived from some ob ject, event, or state
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘benefit’ or ‘beneficial’ is often ‘that which helps.’ Accordingly, in ⟦1 Timothy 4:8|1 Timothy 4:8⟧ one may render ἡ γὰρ σωματικὴ γυμνασία πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐστὶν ὠφέλιμος as ‘physical exercise helps to a small extent’ or ‘if one exercises one’s body, that helps a little.’

s.dp: Help, Care For › Serve
s.d: to serve with a view to impressing others
s.g: eyeservice; to serve in order to call attention to oneself

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: eye, normally including the eyelids
s.c: In a number of languages an important distinction is made between the eyes consisting of the eyeballs and the eyes covered or partially covered by the eyelids. In ⟦Matthew 9:29|Matthew 9:29⟧ and ⟦Matthew 20:34|Matthew 20:34⟧, Jesus apparently touched the eyelids, not the eyeballs.

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὀφθαλμός<SDBG:ὀφθαλμός:000000>}[a] ‘eye,’ {D:8.23}) the capacity to see

s.dp: Understand › Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὀφθαλμός<SDBG:ὀφθαλμός:000000>}[a] ‘eye,’ {D:8.23}) capacity to understand as the result of perception
s.g: to be able to understand; to come to perceive; understanding
s.c: In both ⟦Luke 19:42|Luke 19:42⟧ and ⟦Ephesians 1:18|Ephesians 1:18⟧ ὀφθαλμός designates a faculty of understanding and is not a reference merely to perception. In ⟦Ephesians 1:18|Ephesians 1:18⟧ καρδία denotes the mind (see LN 26.3), so that the phrase ‘the eyes of the mind’ really means ‘the capacity for understanding which the mind has.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Envy, Jealousy
s.d: (an idiom, literally: evil eye) a feeling of jealousy and resentment because of what someone else has or does
s.c: It is also possible to understand ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός in ⟦Matthew 20:15|Matthew 20:15⟧ as meaning ‘stinginess’ (see LN 57.108). See also LN 23.149.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Give
s.d: (an idiom, literally: evil eye) to be stingy
s.c: It is also possible that ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός in ⟦Matthew 20:15|Matthew 20:15⟧ is to be understood in the sense of ‘jealous’ (see LN 88.165). See also LN 23.149.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: (idioms, literally: their eyes were weighed down) to become excessively or exceedingly sleepy
s.g: to have become very sleepy; to be very sleepy
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ἦσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ βεβαρημένοι (or καταβαρυνόμενοι) would be ‘they could no longer keep their eyes open’ or ‘they could not drive sleep away.’

s.dp: Learn › Be Willing To Learn
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to close the eyes) to be unwilling to learn and to evaluate something fairly
s.g: to refuse to learn; to refuse to recognize
s.c: In a number of languages there is a problem involved in a literal rendering of ‘to close the eyes,’ since this may be understood in a strictly literal sense or as denoting death.

s.dp: Understand › Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to blind the eyes) to cause someone to no longer have the capacity for understanding
s.g: to cause to not understand; to make unable to comprehend
s.c: Though in some languages there is a close relationship between the eyes and comprehension, in many languages it is simply impossible to use the idiom ‘to blind the eyes’ in speaking of ‘causing someone not to understand.’ The problem becomes particularly difficult in speaking of ‘darkness blinding the eyes’ as in ⟦1 John 2:11|1 John 2:11⟧. People can understand how ‘bright light would blind the eyes,’ but it would be strange indeed to think of ‘darkness’ having such an effect. In the context of ⟦1 John 2:11|1 John 2:11⟧, the darkness is, of course, not literal darkness but a state of sinfulness. Therefore, in some languages it may be necessary to translate ‘their sinfulness has made it impossible for them to understand’ or ‘because they sin, they cannot understand.’

s.dp: Animals › Reptiles and Other 'Creeping Things'
s.d: long legless reptile; no eyelids or external ears; moves by wriggling or gliding; some species have a poisonous bite; symbol of lurking, unexpected danger; associated with lies, deception, and misleading teaching
s.c: Though ὄφις may refer to any kind of snake, in ⟦Luke 10:19|Luke 10:19⟧ it is obviously a reference to a poisonous snake that would harm a person who stepped on it. In translating ⟦Luke 10:19|Luke 10:19⟧ it is essential to avoid an expression which will mean merely ‘to walk on snakes’ as though one were to walk for some distance over a mass of swarming snakes. The implication of this context is simply that one is able to step on snakes without being harmed.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὄφις<SDBG:ὄφις:000000>}[a] snake, {D:4.52}) a dangerous and despised person
s.c: One must exercise due caution in rendering ἔχιδνα in ⟦Matthew 12:34|Matthew 12:34⟧ and ὄφις in ⟦Matthew 23:33|Matthew 23:33⟧, since in some cultures snakes are regarded as being particularly wise and clever, and therefore an expression such as ‘brood of vipers’ could be a compliment. In some languages important distinctions are made between different types of snakes, and therefore connotations may vary considerably.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Elevated Land Formations
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὀφρῦς ‘brow,’ not occurring in the NT) the upper portion of a precipitous or steep contour of a hill or mountain

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Cause Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to cause hardship by continual annoyance

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › General
s.d: to cause a crowd to gather
s.g: to gather a crowd or to cause a crowd to form
s.c: The context of ⟦Acts 17:5|Acts 17:5⟧ indicates clearly that the crowd was an unruly and undisciplined gathering of people, and therefore one may often employ an expression equivalent to ‘they gathered together a mob.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › General
s.d: a casual non-membership group of people, fairly large in size and assembled for whatever purpose{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages there is no term corresponding to ‘crowd.’ One may, however, usually speak of such a group of people as ‘many people’ or ‘many men and women.’ Depending on the context, it may besary to indicate some relative difference in size, for example, ‘very large crowd’ or ‘many, many people.’ If the crowd is relatively small, one may sometimes speak of ‘just some people.’

s.dp: Status › Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
s.d: the common people, in contrast with those who are rich, leaders, and/or authorities in the society, often with the implication of disdain and low esteem
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘the common people’ is ‘the poor people,’ but in some languages an equivalent depends upon geographical location, for example, ‘those who live on the edge of town’ (the opposite situation from what exists in most present-day metropolitan centers). In still other languages ‘the common people’ may be designated in terms of lack of status, for example, ‘those who have no position’ or ‘those whom the rich do not greet’ or ‘those before whom no one ever bows.’

s.dp: Constructions › Buildings
s.d: a strong military fortification
s.c: The term ὀχύρωμα occurs in the NT only in ⟦2 Corinthians 10:4|2 Corinthians 10:4⟧, where it is used figuratively of the strength of false arguments. In a number of languages it may be more satisfactory to render ὀχύρωμα as a kind of simile so as to mark this figurative usage, for example, ‘powerful weapons with which to destroy false arguments in the same way that people would destroy fortresses.’ In some languages a ‘fortress’ may be described in terms of its function, for example, ‘a place for protection’ or ‘a place to defend oneself.’ Often, however, a fortress is described in terms of its construction, for example, ‘a strong-walled place.’

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: fish intended for food or the flesh of fish as food
s.c: In Greek the usual meaning of ὀψάριον is a tidbit of food eaten with bread, but it occurs in later Greek in the meaning of fish, and in the NT this meaning occurs only in the fourth Gospel (compare the usage in ⟦John 6:9|John 6:9⟧ with ἰχθύς in parallel passages).|Many languages distinguish clearly between terms for fish while still living in the water and fish which have been caught and presumably are to be used for food.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Units of Time: Daybreak, Midday, Midnight, Late
s.d: pertaining to a point near the end of a day (normally after sunset but before night)
s.c: It is also possible to understand ὀψέ in ⟦Mark 11:19|Mark 11:19⟧ as indicating a period of time, namely ‘evening’ (see LN 67.197).

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: the period after sunset and before darkness (compare {D:67.191})

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time subsequent to another point of time, with the implication of relative lateness

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Rain
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὄψιος<SDBG:ὄψιος:000000>} ‘late,’ {D:67.76}, and used absolutely of ‘late rain’) a rain that comes late in the season, that is to say, in April or May after the normal rains of the winter season have passed
s.c: See πρόϊμος ‘early rain’ (LN 14.14) for a discussion of problems involving ‘late rain’ and ‘early rain.’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Units of Time: Daybreak, Midday, Midnight, Late
